lead: A difference equation is the discrete-time twin of a differential equation. It ties the present output sample to a few past output samples and to present and past input samples, using fixed numbers as coefficients. Give it a handful of starting values and you can compute every later sample with a loop — which is exactly what a digital filter does inside a phone, a hearing aid or an ECG monitor. The roots of its characteristic equation decide whether the output settles or blows up. This chapter works entirely in the time domain.
prereq: You need: 5.5 for the convolution sum and impulse response, and Unit 1 for the unit step, unit impulse and signal shifting.

sections.h3: The equation, its order and its two cases

blocks.text: A discrete-time LTI system can be described by a linear constant-coefficient difference equation. Writing every output term on the left and every input term on the right gives the standard form:
y[n] = −Σ<sub>k=1…N</sub> a<sub>k</sub> y[n − k] + Σ<sub>m=0…M</sub> b<sub>m</sub> x[n − m]
blocks.where: y[n] is the output sample at index n; x[n] is the input sample; a<sub>k</sub> and b<sub>m</sub> are real constants, so the system is time-invariant; N is the order; M is the number of past input samples used.

blocks.text: The order N is the largest delay of the output in the equation. It is also the number of past outputs you must store and the number of unit delays in the hardware. The coefficients must be plain numbers: a term such as n·y[n−1] or y[n]·y[n−1] destroys linearity or time-invariance.

If at least one ak is nonzero, the output feeds back into itself. The system is recursive, and its impulse response lasts forever, so it is called IIR (infinite impulse response). If every ak = 0, then y[n] = Σ bm x[n − m], which is the convolution sum of 5.5 with h[n] = bn for 0 ≤ n ≤ M. That is a non-recursive, or FIR (finite impulse response), filter.

To start the recursion you need the N past outputs y[−1], y[−2], …, y[−N]. These are the initial conditions. Rest initial conditions means y[n] = 0 for all n < 0: the system was silent before the input arrived.

items: Move each a<sub>k</sub> y[n − k] to the right side with its sign changed, so y[n] stands alone.
Write down the initial conditions y[−1] … y[−N].
Put n = 0, substitute the input sample and the initial conditions, and get y[0].
Raise n by one, substitute the value just found, and repeat. Every step uses only numbers you already have.

sections.h3: Block diagram: adders, delays and multipliers

blocks.text: Three blocks build every such equation. An adder (Σ) sums its inputs. A multiplier scales a signal by a constant. A unit delay holds one sample: its output is y[n−1] when its input is y[n]. Textbooks label the delay z⁻¹, read as z inverse; the symbol comes from the Z-transform in Unit 6, but here it only means one sample of memory.

A direct-form diagram of order N uses N delays, one adder and up to N + M + 1 multipliers. The figure shows the first-order case y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n−1], so b₀ = 1, a₁ = −0.5 and the feedback path multiplies by −a₁ = 0.5. Each new output sample is delayed, scaled and added back to the input. A non-recursive FIR system has no feedback path at all: only a chain of delays and multipliers feeding one large adder.

sections.h3: Closed form: natural plus forced response

blocks.text: Iteration gives numbers, not a formula. The closed form has two parts: the natural response, the system's own behaviour with the input removed, and the forced response, its steady reaction to the input.
Natural response. Set the input to zero and try y[n] = λⁿ. Substituting and multiplying by λ<sup>N</sup> gives the characteristic equation:

blocks.where: λ are the natural modes; a₀ is the coefficient of y[n], normally 1; N is the order, so there are N roots counting repeats.

blocks.text: Each distinct root λ<sub>i</sub> contributes a term C<sub>i</sub>λ<sub>i</sub><sup>n</sup>. That same λ<sub>i</sub> is a pole of the system. A root repeated r times contributes (C₀ + C₁n + … + C<sub>r−1</sub>n<sup>r−1</sup>)λⁿ.

Forced response. Guess a form like the input and substitute: a constant input gives a constant guess A, an input 2ⁿ gives A·2ⁿ, a sinusoid gives A cos(ωn) + B sin(ωn). Solve for the constants algebraically.

Total response: y[n] = y<sub>nat</sub>[n] + y<sub>forced</sub>[n] for n ≥ 0. Find the N unknown C<sub>i</sub> from y[−1] … y[−N], or from y[0] … y[N−1] if you obtained those by iterating first. N conditions fix N constants.
A causal system is BIBO stable if every bounded input gives a bounded output. For a difference equation that happens exactly when every natural mode decays:

blocks.where: λ<sub>i</sub> are the characteristic roots, also called poles; |·| is the magnitude of a complex number; the statement is for a causal system, whose modes start at n = 0.

blocks.text: The unit circle is |z| = 1 in the z-plane: inside means stable, on means marginal, outside means unstable. A real negative root close to −1 gives an alternating slow decay — the ringing heard after a click in an audio filter. Complex roots on the circle give a pure oscillation at ω = angle of the root.

The Z-transform in Unit 6 gets the same answer faster: H(z) = B(z)/A(z), poles at the roots of A(z), and a table gives the inverse. The time-domain work here shows what the machine does sample by sample, and it is the method to use when only the first few outputs are wanted.

figure.caption: The output y[n] goes through a unit delay and a 0.5 multiplier and returns to the adder, so every new sample reuses the last one. Follow the loop once and you see why the response never stops by itself.

spec.title: First-order recursive system
spec.aria: Block diagram of y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n−1]: the output goes through a unit delay and a 0.5 multiplier and returns to the adder.

examples.question: A causal discrete-time system is described by y[n] − 0.5y[n − 1] = x[n], with input x[n] = u[n] and rest initial conditions y[n] = 0 for n < 0. (a) Iterate the equation for n = 0 to 3. (b) Find the closed form y[n]. (c) State whether the system is stable.
steps: Rewrite in recursive form: y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n − 1]. Here a₁ = −0.5, so the feedback coefficient is −a₁ = 0.5.
Characteristic equation: λ − 0.5 = 0, so the single root is λ = 0.5. Natural response: C(0.5)ⁿ.
Forced response: try the constant A. Then A − 0.5A = 1, giving 0.5A = 1 and A = 2. Check: 2 − 0.5(2) = 1, correct.
Total: y[n] = 2 + C(0.5)ⁿ. Apply y[0] = 1: 2 + C = 1, so C = −1.
Closed form: y[n] = 2 − (0.5)ⁿ for n ≥ 0. At n = 3 this gives 2 − 0.125 = 1.875, matching the iteration.
The pole is at 0.5, and |0.5| < 1, so it lies inside the unit circle: the system is stable and y[n] settles at 2.
examples.answer: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1.5, y[2] = 1.75, y[3] = 1.875, and y[n] = 2 − (0.5)ⁿ for n ≥ 0; the pole at 0.5 is inside the unit circle, so the system is stable and settles at 2.
examples.check:
a1 = 0.5
y = 0.0
for n in range(4):
    y = a1 * y + 1.0
    print(y)
for n in range(4):
    print(2 - 0.5 ** n)
print(a1)

traps: Sign slip: y[n] + a₁y[n−1] = x[n] becomes y[n] = −a₁y[n−1] + x[n]. The multiplier in the feedback path is −a₁, never a₁.
Wrong starting sample: begin from y[−1], not y[0]. Starting at y[0] shifts the entire output sequence by one place.
Characteristic equation for y[n] − 0.5y[n−1] = x[n] is λ − 0.5 = 0, so λ = 0.5. Writing 1 − 0.5λ = 0 gives λ = 2 and a false unstable answer.
Order versus input length: N counts output delays, M counts input delays. A second-order equation can carry any number of b coefficients.
A repeated root on the unit circle grows like n and is unstable. Only single roots on the circle are marginally stable — the examiner's favourite trap.

quiz.q: Define the order of a difference equation and say what it counts.
quiz.a: The order N is the largest delay of the output y[n−k] present in the equation. It equals the number of past outputs stored and the number of unit delays needed.

quiz.q: Why is a non-recursive difference equation called FIR?
quiz.a: When every a_k = 0 nothing feeds back, so y[n] is a finite weighted sum of x[n], x[n−1], …, x[n−M]. The impulse response h[n] = b_n lasts only M+1 samples.

quiz.q: For y[n] = 0.5y[n−1] + x[n] with x[n] = δ[n] and y[−1] = 0, find y[0], y[1], y[2] and the impulse response.
quiz.a: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5, y[2] = 0.25; h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n], which decays to zero, so the system is stable.

quiz.q: A causal second-order system has characteristic roots λ = 0.8 and λ = −1.2. Is it stable?
quiz.a: No. |−1.2| = 1.2 > 1, so the mode (−1.2)ⁿ grows without bound. One root outside the unit circle is enough to make the system unstable.

quiz.q: A causal system has single roots at λ = +j and λ = −j. Describe the output behaviour.
quiz.a: Both magnitudes equal 1 and the roots are simple, so the system is marginally stable. The modes give a pure oscillation of fixed amplitude at ω = π/2, with no growth and no decay.

quiz.q: Why can a low-order recursive filter produce a long impulse response with few multipliers, and what does that cost?
quiz.a: Feedback reuses one stored sample many times, so a second-order section needs about five multipliers per sample however long the response is. The cost is sensitivity: rounding the coefficients moves the poles and can make the filter noisy or unstable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every real-time audio equaliser, pacemaker filter and telecom echo canceller runs a difference equation like this in fixed-point arithmetic. Rounding the coefficients shifts the poles slightly, so designers check the pole radius after rounding, not before. Search the terms direct form I and II, biquad, fixed-point pole sensitivity and all-pass filter design to see the industrial versions. Control engineers meet the same equation as a discrete state-space model, where the characteristic roots appear as eigenvalues of the state matrix.
